title: Hello Kitty ready to keep you company in the bathroom with new dessert-aroma Sanrio toilet paper
description: It’s like a skating party in your bathroom, and all your Sanrio friends are invited. content:
It’s like a skating party in your bathroom, and all your Sanrio friends are invited.

Part of the secret to the enduring popularity of Hello Kitty and her Sanrio pals is what loyal friends they are. Sure, you could take the cynical interpretation that their incredibly wide variety of character merch is simply a way to multiply revenue streams, but there’s no denying that it also means that almost no matter what you’re doing in life, there’s a way for you to do it with your favorite Sanrio characters keeping you company…even in the bathroom.

This week, Fukuoka-based paper products company Marutomi Seishi began selling its newest collaboration with Sanrio, the “Sanrio Winter 12-Roll Double.” And yes, that’s “double” as in “double-ply toilet paper.” This isn’t just a case of playful packaging, either, the paper itself is covered in illustrations.

▼ It’s only fitting that Sanrio toilet paper be as kind and gentle as the characters that appear on it.

Over a dozen Sanrio characters are featured, including Helloy Kitty, Pompompurin, Cinnamoroll, My Melody, Kuromi, Pochacco, and Hangyodon, on two patterns.

The new paper has a wintery motif, depicting the Sanrio friends bundled up for an ice skating outing rendered in a cool snowy color scheme.

Marutomi Seishi also promises that the Sanrio toiler paper has a “sweets fragrance.” That’s not to be confused with a generic “sweet” smell, but instead appears to indicate that this toilet paper has the aroma of some sort of dessert.

The goal, Marutomi Seishi says, is for the Sanrio toilet paper to “create a peaceful, tranquil atmosphere in your bathroom,” and the 12-roll pack should be showing up now in Japanese drugstores and other housewares retailers.

title: Cinnabon gets into the Japanese spirit with new Wagokorobon treats
description: Cinnabon Japan finds two new ways to mix its own dessert traditions with Japan’s. content:
Cinnabon Japan finds two new ways to mix its own dessert traditions with Japan’s.

Unlike some other American sweets suppliers who’ve set up shop in Japan, Cinnabon doesn’t have Japan-exclusive menu items all that often. We can probably chalk that up to the chain’s key ingredient, cinnamon, being a distinct flavor that doesn’t feature very often at all in traditional Japanese desserts. Leave the cinnamon in, and it’s hard to find a cordial combo with Japanese ingredients, but take it out, and it’s not really a cinnamon bun anymore, is it?

But every now and again Cinnabon Japan does find a way to create new desserts with Japanese inspirations, and it’s got two on its menu right now.

Collectively called the Wagokorobon line (wagokoro meaning “Japanese heart”), the first of the two items is the Kuri (Chestnut) Matcha Mini Chocobon. This starts as one of Cinnabon’s cinnamon-light Chocobons, which get chocolate kneaded into the standard Cinnabon dough plus a drizzle of chocolate sauce. This Wagokorobon version also gets a chestnut frosting, representing one of Japan’s favorite fall dessert flavors, plus a whole lot of matcha sprinkled on top. There’s so much green tea that it looks like it’ll definitely impart a noticeable texture, but that powdery sensation shouldn’t be too far off from the sprinkled cinnamon on conventional cinnamon buns.

Meanwhile, there’s a different granular guest star on the Kuromitsu Kinako Minibon: kinako, or roasted soybean powder. While not as sweet as the sweet red bean paste called anko that often shows up in Japanese confectioneries, kinako is noticeably sweet and fragrant, with a slight nutty quality to its flavor. Kinako’s texture is fine enough that it can make the things it’s sprinkled on feel a little dry, though, so it’s often accompanied by kuromitsu, a kind of Japanese brown sugar molasses, as it is here, and the mix of sweet, sticky, powdery sensations should slot very nicely into what you’d want from a cinnamon bun while still having an unmistakably Japanese taste.

Both Wagokorobon items are on sale at Cinnabon Japan branches now, and are scheduled to be available until late November.

Enjoy the taste of freshly whisked matcha at the touch of a button.

Japan is home to many different types of vending machines, and some of the most impressive are the ones that serve freshly ground coffee, with the beans ground and each cup brewed to order inside the machine. The process is even shown live on a monitor, so customers can watch their coffee being prepared.

Now, Toyo Vending, the company behind the popular Mill-Ground Coffee vending machines, has teamed up with tea giant Ito En to bring this technology to powdered green tea. The result is “Japan Quality Matcha”, a new style of drink that uses carefully selected matcha ingredients and specialised preparation technology to deliver an authentic taste similar to freshly whisked matcha, with five different strengths to choose from.

The new machines aim to cater to the growing demand for matcha, making it even more accessible and convenient, particularly for overseas visitors. Unlike regular drink vending machines, which are filled with bottles and cans, these ones prepare drinks to order, with the process beginning only after the customer presses the button. The company says its technology produces a taste similar to freshly whisked matcha, while also allowing customers to choose how strong they want their drink.

The machines are easy to spot, with three different all-green designs, each of which takes its inspiration from Japanese scenery and traditional culture. The first design features a deep green colour inspired by Japanese landscapes, designed to evoke a sense of tranquillity and relaxation.

The second features traditional Japanese patterns, while the third, described as “Modern Luxury”, combines a large display screen with an image of matcha against a premium tea plantation. The machines are set to be located at high-traffic locations like expressway rest areas, train stations, airports, commercial facilities, and tourist destinations popular with international visitors.

These machines are an exciting new way to enjoy matcha, and are already beginning to generate a lot of buzz in Japan. Their uniqueness has been summed up by Toyo Vending CEO Yoshimasa Wakamatsu, who has this message for matcha fans.

“We have always been committed to providing an uncompromising cup of coffee through our Mill-Ground Coffee machines, and now we’ve applied that same technology to matcha, one of Japan’s traditional treasures. We’re delighted to have found such an excellent partner in Ito En and to be able to deliver authentic Japan Quality to customers both in Japan and overseas. Through the familiarity of vending machines, we hope to offer a new way to experience matcha.”

We certainly can’t wait to try the new matcha, and all five different strengths that allow you to select your preferred intensity, when they begin appearing around Japan this month. With a variety of options to choose from, including regular matcha and matcha lattes, these look set to become the next hot trend to flood your socials, so keep an eye out for them during your travels.

title: Restaurant opens in Japan with all-dementia waitresses, serves up ramen, awareness, and kindness
description: Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is upfront about potential problems in order to cultivate future understanding. Japan has incredibly high customer service standards, especially where restaurants are concerned. Because of that, a restaurant saying, in advance, that it might get your order wrong seems like a recipe for dissatisfied diners, but that strategy led to smiles […]
content:
Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is upfront about potential problems in order to cultivate future understanding.

Japan has incredibly high customer service standards, especially where restaurants are concerned. Because of that, a restaurant saying, in advance, that it might get your order wrong seems like a recipe for dissatisfied diners, but that strategy led to smiles all around, plus a few appreciative tears, recently in the city of Matsuyama, Ehime Prefecture.

“Restaurant of Mistaken Orders” didn’t get its unusual name through a translation error, as that really is a pretty accurate rendering of its Japanese name, Chumon wo Machigaeru Kamoshirenai Ryori-ten. That less-than-perfect precision isn’t due to a lack of effort or concern on the restaurant’s part, though, but because the waitstaff is composed of senior citizens with dementia.

Restaurant of Mistaken Orders, which started out in 2018, operates on a popup basis, partnering with preexisting restaurants which serve as a venue for the unique eatery for the day. For its most recent iteration in Matsuyama, Restaurant of Mistaken Orders teamed up with Tenryu Ramen on September 21, which was both the Japanese public holiday Respect for the Aged Day and World Alzheimer’s Day.

▼ Restaurant of Mistaken Orders at Tenryu Ramen

It should be pointed out that the driving philosophy behind Restaurant of Mistaken Orders is not “Let’s get those dementia-stricken seniors working!” Instead, the purpose of the venture is to foster a greater sense of awareness and consideration towards people living with dementia, and also to give the participating seniors a sense of confidence and accomplishment by showing that their condition doesn’t have to mean complete debilitation and isolation from human interaction. “We hope this feeling of openness and understanding will spread across Japan, and through the world” says the organization in is mission statement, showing that the restaurant setting is meant to serve as a sort of metaphor for kindness wherever one may encounter someone with dementia.

In Matsuyama, four local seniors, ranging in age from 78 to 88, took orders and served diners, including the daughter and granddaughter of one of the participants (the daughter is the woman who can be seen wiping away tears in the above video, while talking about how emotionally moving it is to see her mother staying active). “If we took our time and listened and spoke patiently, we could understand each other,” says a father of a family of four that are at Restaurant of Mistaken Orders of communicating with the staff, and one of the elderly waitresses, at the end of the event, said with a smile “I was really happy to get to see so many people and talk with them.”

▼ The project’s concept video

With community outreach and public awareness being the primary goals, operating profits aren’t really a priority for Restaurant of Mistaken Orders, and the organization accepts online donations here for those that aren’t able to come in for a bite to eat, but still want to lend a helping hand.

title: Get the taste of the U.K. in Tokyo with 99 Flakes, meat pies, and Jaffa Cakes
description: This tiny Shibuya spot brings quintessential UK snacks straight to central Tokyo. content:
This tiny Shibuya spot brings quintessential UK snacks straight to central Tokyo.

Whether you have moved to a different country and pining for the foodstuffs of the motherland or you are interested in foreign cuisine without the hefty price tag of the airfare, specialty import stores are a treat to walk around. Tucked away amid the towering buildings of Shibuya, you’ll find The British Shop, a grocery store specializing in British ingredients with its own eat-in area.

Located just outside exit B3 of the Shibuya subway station, The British Shop’s footprint is even smaller than a convenience store, but the shelves are lined with British foods and a table is set up in the center from which you can enjoy a variety of foods.

One of the highlights for a nostalgic Brit would be the ice cream van staple of a 99 Flake, essentially a soft-serve ice cream cone with a Cadbury’s Flake chocolate bar inserted into it.

Unfortunately, sales were suspended on the day we visited, but we still got to enjoy some chocolatey goodness with our ice cream.

To satisfy our ice cream cravings, we opted for a double scoop (750 yen [US$4.74]) along with a Flake (100 yen): the first scoop was vanilla and clotted cream, and the second blackcurrant and double cream.

While clotted cream is an indispensable accompaniment to scones, it has to be said that seeing it as an ice cream flavor is pretty unusual. The taste was unexpectedly light with a gentle sweetness, reproducing the lightness of actual clotted cream. Combining a subtly milky taste with the rich aroma of vanilla made for an addictive, delicious flavor.

Blackcurrant is known as ‘cassis’ in Japan, where it is arguably seen most as a part of alcoholic drinks, but in the UK it is much more widely enjoyed in squashes (fruit cordials) or as a component to desserts. The tartness of the ice cream wasn’t too strong, and had a taste that made us keep coming back in for another scoop.

After spending any amount of time in Japan, you come to realize that ‘pies’ are almost always of the dessert variety, often containing fruits, but at this little shop you can purchase the Chunky Beef Pie for 600 yen, which is made with huge chunks of diced beef and has a very rich taste.

After coming all the way to the store, it would be unthinkable if you left without picking up some snacks as a souvenir, and what better way to do that than to take home the subject of Britain’s biggest snack debate: the Jaffa Cake (520 yen).

Delectable treats made by layering a soft sponge cake with a sweet-and-sour orange filling and coating it with chocolate, these once featured as the main focus in a legal case to determine whether they were actually biscuits (cookies) or, indeed as the name would suggest, cakes. Spoiler: they’re cakes. Since Jaffa Cakes are hard to find in Japan, these are a must-grab item if you visit the shop, and being sweet they make a perfect accompaniment to a cup of tea.

Next up were the Somerset Cheddar and Shallot flavor Savoursmiths crisps.

A high-end crisp brand from the UK comes at a price of 220 yen for a bag, which is definitely on the higher side when comparing other potato chips in a Japanese supermarket. The crunchy texture was exquisite, and we ended up finishing them before we had even realized it.

Sometimes a trip to Tokyo is not easy, so there’s also the option of ordering from the shop online, where shipping is free on orders over 12,000 yen.

The British Shop offers everything from classic snacks to slightly niche ingredients, with items such as bacon, bread, seasonings, and Yorkshire Tea Gold all available to purchase.  If you’re not as unlucky as us when visiting the store, you’ll also get to try the quintessential British summertime treat of a 99 Flake all the way on the other side of the globe.

title: Japanese government hires leading comedy agency to explain national defense spending
description: The number one rule of comedy is unwavering loyalty to the government. I suppose in terms of things on a global scale, the Japanese government isn’t doing all that bad. It’s just that with all the talk of how Prime Minister Takaichi works constantly and rarely sleeps, I was sort of expecting something more in […]
content:
The number one rule of comedy is unwavering loyalty to the government.

I suppose in terms of things on a global scale, the Japanese government isn’t doing all that bad. It’s just that with all the talk of how Prime Minister Takaichi works constantly and rarely sleeps, I was sort of expecting something more in the way of results. 

Don’t get me wrong, since coming into power, her cabinet pissed off China right quick, jacked up visa fees, and made it so people can’t poop on the flag. These are all indeed things that were done, and yet, all those efforts don’t seem to have changed the fact that the cost of living in Japan keeps going up and that entire cities are on the verge of being taken over by bears and monkeys.

One other thing the Takaichi cabinet has been hard at work at is amending the constitution of Japan to give the military more freedom to take action in overseas conflicts that may not directly threaten the safety of this country. Opponents of this idea say that it goes against the principles of Japan’s previously pacifist constitution, but maybe this is just a very complex situation in an increasingly destabilized world, which may have aspects not everyone is aware of. If only there was a sassy comedy duo that could explain it all in terms an average Joe can understand!

And just like that, our prayers are answered. The Government Public Relations Office has teamed up with Japan’s leading comedy talent agency Yoshimoto Kogyo to produce a campaign that explains why some of the seemingly uninspiring things the government’s been doing are actually very good.

Yoshimoto specializes in the style of comedy known as manzai. This is a bit of a throwback to the vaudeville era of Western comedy, often involving duos wherein one is the straight man (tsukkomi) and the other the funny man (boke). This particular series seems to employ a Burns and Allen style combo featuring the husband Kunio and wife Tamiyo, as they trade quips over national policy.

▼ A video trailer for the campaign

The art of manzai is largely associated with the culture of Osaka, and is often best delivered in an Osaka dialect and accent, which I prefer to liken to a Staten Island accent, more or less based on vibes alone. There are currently seven pages where Kunio and Tamiyo crack wise about national policy in this manner of speaking, so let’s take a look at their talk about national defense.

Tamiyo: “Did you know that Japan’s support ships help sustain our daily lives? They support the world, and Japan is supported as well.”

Kunio: “Actually, more than 80 percent of the ships they protect belong to other countries! Japan helps to safeguard its allies, so the world protects Japan in return. We work together and look out for one another, ya know?”

…

Oh, that’s it? Hahahaha!

Granted, it’s hard to make cooperative maritime defense funny, or at least, it’s hard when your job is being a government mouthpiece. Let’s see how they handle some softball topics like the space program instead.

Tamiyo: “You ever take it for granted that we can go places we’ve never been before and don’t get lost?”

Kunio: “Actually, we’re being guided from space. Japan’s Michibiki satellite system provides us with directions around the clock.”

…

Sorry, I was thinking about something else there. That one was quite a whiff too, wasn’t it? Alright, let’s take a look at their hot take on AI. This should be a slam dunk since the characters appear to have been hastily generated by AI themselves.

Tamiyo: “You think since AI can help with things like planning meals or finding information, it can also be useful for national security?”

Kunio: “Actually, efforts are underway to leverage AI so that it can help safeguard the nation.”

…

Jeez, they’re hardly even using an Osaka dialect in these. Getting a comedy routine down solid is hard work and takes time. We can at least see the seeds of the mansplaining premise beginning to sprout. It all makes me wonder if maybe I’m being too hard on the comedic stylings of Tamiyo and Kunio. Let’s see what online comments say about them.

“Are they trying to brainwash us with propaganda now?”
“The all-knowing man teaching his dimwitted wife. This really encapsulates why Japan ranks 114th out of 145 countries in the Global Gender Gap Index.”
“This is the lowest form of propaganda. I’m done supporting Yoshimoto and won’t buy anything their performers do commercials for.”
“They clearly think the public is stupid. They’re looking down on all of us.”
“They must think we’re insanely gullible.”
“It seems that the country is the role of the ‘husband,’ and the people are the ‘wife,’ which is also just creepy.”
“There is no way this will foster understanding. Stop it immediately.”
“Don’t waste our tax money on this garbage. If the Prime Minister would just show up in the Diet to provide proper answers or hold actual press conferences, this wouldn’t be necessary!”
“This is very dystopian.”

I scrolled far and wide and could not find anyone with an even remotely positive thing to say about this campaign. It does not bode well for the government, whose recent lifting of a ban on exporting lethal weapons is currently opposed by about 57 percent of the population, according to a poll by Japan’s Kyodo news organization. Kyodo also cites sources inside the government as saying that explanations of policy that avoid words like “lethal” would be more effective in swaying public opinion. 

That does sound a tad Orwellian, but we shouldn’t knock it till we try it, so let’s see what Tamiyo and Kunio have to say about the nation’s defense policy.

Tamiyo: “You ever think we take uneventful days for granted?”

Kunio: “Actually, the fact that nothing newsworthy happened today just goes to show ya. A day where ‘nothing happens’ ain’t no coincidence. It’s the result of tireless work to keep us safe.”

Ha! Those two kill me.

Source: Public Relations Office – Government of Japan, PR Times, Kyodo, My Game News Flash

This leak-proof stainless steel bottle has a sleek and simple design, with a handle built into the lid for easy carrying. The body has a pale white colour that shimmers delicately in the light, adding an air of sophistication to your everyday drinking experience.

This is one of the four items in the series that’s also eligible for Starbucks’ online store name engraving service, which lets you add your name and/or a pictogram to the back, bringing the total to 7,450 yen.

The body of this stainless steel tumbler has a soothing mint green hue, while the shape is inspired by Starbucks’ paper cups, making it suitable for a wide range of scenarios, from everyday use to office settings.

This product is also eligible for the online store’s personalisation service, which raises the price to 5,700 yen.

▼ Mint Green Logo Cold Cup Tumbler – 710 millilitres (3,050 yen)

This tumbler features an eye-catching, diamond-cut design that gives off a different look depending on how the light hits it.

The new collection is a beautiful way to add a sense of warmth and luxury to wintry drinks, and they can be purchased at Starbucks stores and online while stocks last.

content:
The “Everyone Gather Together! Winter Pokémon Campaign” goes all out for the 30th anniversary celebrations.

It’s become something of an annual tradition for Mister Donut to release a new Pokémon collection at the end of the year, with a different pocket monster taking centre stage as the star of the show. This year, however, for Pokémon’s 30th anniversary, the chain is going all out with the celebrations, putting not just one Pokémon in the spotlight, but a whole gathering from past campaigns.

▼ The promo image reads “Atsumare! Minna!” (“Gather! Everyone!”)

Image: Press release

With this being the ninth Pokémon x Mister Donut collaboration collection, there are a lot of characters returning for the celebrations, and Mister Donut says every Pokémon that has appeared in previous collaborations will be coming together for this year’s collection. Leading the charge on the doughnut front is Alolan Diglett, who differs from the Diglett that appeared previously with a different coating and a gummy nose instead of a chocolate one.

▼ Oh, and a chocolate rendering of its head tuft, seeing as it’s Alolan.

The theme for this year’s collaboration is “Alolan Diglett Brings Everyone Together!” and while the doughnuts are limited to Alolan Diglett and fan favourite Pikachu, the Pokémon gathering takes place on the limited-edition merchandise that can be bought as a set with the doughnuts. There’s also a cream-filled choux doughnut called “Pokémon Friends Gather! Angel & Custard“, which comes in one of four randomly selected sleeves featuring the Pokémon characters.

The “Goods Set” (2,200 yen for takeout, 2,217 yen for dine-in) gets you two Pokémon doughnuts of your choice, one doughnut from a choice of two “Pon de Wreath” varieties, a choice of one of two blankets, and an original paper bag. The “Kids Goods Set” gets you one Pokémon doughnut, one doughnut from the choice of two “Pon de Wreath” varieties, a limited-edition Pokémon glass and an original paper bag.

▼ We stopped by to get our hands on the “Goods Set”, which came in this gorgeous bag.

When we returned home, we laid out our haul, and couldn’t help but admire the cute characters that sat in front of use, including on the doughnut box.

Taking a closer look at the blanket, there are two to choose from, blue and orange, and we went for the orange one, which features plenty of Grass-type Pokémon and other warm-coloured characters. Each blanket has a different selection of Pokémon, so you can either choose the one that has your favourite characters, or purchase two sets to catch ’em all.

The blankets look much the same as they do every year, but this time they seem to have been made slightly bigger. They’ve increased in height, making them closer to square than the horizontally elongated rectangles of previous years, giving you more coverage for use as a lap blanket, which is a welcome improvement. It is rather thin, though, and amounts to around 1,200 yen of the price of the set so it’s not entirely a bargain, but it is an exclusive you won’t find anywhere else so it’s still a sought-after item for fans.

▼ Last year’s blanket on top, compared to this year’s slightly larger version below.

As for the doughnuts, they looked as cute as ever, and Alolan Diglett was particularly delicious, thanks to its chocolate-coated doughnut base and whipped-cream-filled centre.

This year, Pikachu appears in its fluffy form for the second year running, and is still filled with the same whipped cream, with custard-flavoured flakes sprinkled across its surface.

▼ Like last year, Pikachu has rosy pink cheeks, even though they really ought to be red, if we’re going to be true to the character.

Both doughnuts were as cute as they were delicious, but the party doesn’t end there, as Mister Donut says it will be bringing out a Slowpoke doughnut to join the collection from 25 November.

▼ Online reservations for the new doughnut begin on 18 November.

Image: Press release

The current Pokémon collection went on sale across Japan from 4 November, but only in limited stocks so you’ll want to head out early to find them or reserve them through Mister Donut’s online ordering service to ensure you don’t miss out.

title: Discount retailers known for massive bargains releases massive Japanese egg sandwich
description: Don Quijote doubles up its “Peculiar Preference” sandwich. You really don’t have to go very far to find one, as just about every convenience store or supermarket stocks them. But if you […]
content:
Don Quijote doubles up its “Peculiar Preference” sandwich.

Japanese egg sandwiches have recently become an unexpected hit among the international foodie community, but within Japan, they’ve been a staple for generations. You really don’t have to go very far to find one, as just about every convenience store or supermarket stocks them.

But if you really love Japan’s egg sandwiches, it’s worth going to the little extra trouble of making a trip to discount retailer Don Quixote to get one, because not only are they massive, right now they’re even bigger than they usually are.

Among tourists, Don Quijote is most famous for their selection of quirky souvenirs and affordable cosmetics, but they also sell clothing, toiletries, housewares, and, at some locations, even food items, including ready to eat bento boxed lunches and sandwiches.

With the chain being popular with a broad range of shoppers, you’d expect them to want to offer foodstuffs that anyone would like. However, for their Henai Meshi, or “Peculiar Preference Food,” line, Don Quijote isn’t worried about fully satisfying everybody. In fact, the goal of Henai Meshi is to create meals “that most people would give 75 points out of 100, but that some people will give 120,” like the Bento with Fried Chicken Skin Only that they offered a while back.

The Henai Meshi egg sandwich isn’t so unusual in terms of it ingredients, but their quantity could be considered egregious by some, as each sandwich is made with two and a half soft-boiled eggs. Right now, though, Don Quijote is running a special promotion in which it’s increasing the size of selected Henai Meshi items, and one of those is the egg sandwich, which has doubled in size and now contains five eggs!

The Five Melty Soft-boiled Egg Sandwich is priced at 430 yen (US$2.70), and if you’re thinking it’s got to be hefty to hold, you’re exactly right. We were curious as to just how heavy it was, so once we got back to the SoraNews24 taste-testing center, before digging in we placed it on a scale…

…which gave us a weight of 418 grams (roughly 14.75 ounces). Granted, a small fraction of that is the plastic packaging, but still, this is close to a pound of eggs and bread. There’s so much egg that the strips of bread between them start to look like garnish, or maybe just something to keep your fingers clean as you eat a whole tray of eggs.

Taste-testing was handled by our Japanese-language reporter P.K. Sanjun, who informs us that, in his estimation, the Five Melty Soft-boiled Egg Sandwich completely misses the mark for the Henai Meshi series. However, that’s not a complaint, because he clarifies that instead of being something that most people would give 75 point to and some would give 120, this sandwich is so delicious that he thinks most people would give it 95 out of a 100.

Of course, while we’re talking about numerical measurements, your dietician probably wouldn’t be too thrilled about what eating five eggs at once would do to your cholesterol levels. However, with Don Quiojote’s double-sized egg sandwich only being available from November 1 to 10, there’s not time really enough time to do all that much dietary damage, making this a decadent special-occasion indulgence P.K. is very happy to have treated himself to.

title: Tokyo to build new crematoriums to meet surging demand
description: Death is a growth industry that no one’s happy about. There has been a lot of talk about the aging population in Japan and how it’s affecting society and the economy. But a more immediate concern is how to handle the influx of people currently dying across the country.  According to estimates, the number of […]
content:
Death is a growth industry that no one’s happy about.

There has been a lot of talk about the aging population in Japan and how it’s affecting society and the economy. But a more immediate concern is how to handle the influx of people currently dying across the country. 

According to estimates, the number of deaths per year is expected to swell to a peak of 1.65 million in 2040, but with the current number over 1.5 million, Japan looks poised to overshoot that estimate considerably. Large cities in particular are starting to feel the strain, since the common method of internment in Japan is cremation. Luckily, this means cemetery space can be kept rather small, but the facilities to perform cremations are limited.

There have been reports of crematoriums in Chiba Prefecture issuing wait times of as many as 10 days, and supply and demand has also seen the costs of such services rise as well. In normal businesses, this would attract other competitors who would eventually bring down prices, but that is especially difficult for crematoriums as they are very costly to set up and zoning laws make it very hard to even find a place to put a facility for burning human remains.

▼ Urayasu Crematorium is located right beside Tokyo Disneyland, you can see just a bit of it if you look to your left along with the Tokyo Skytree in the distance.

Nowhere is this situation more severe then the dense metropolis of Tokyo, whose government recently decided to take matters into their own hands and are drafting a proposal to build a series of small-scale publicly run crematoriums throughout the 23 wards. They will focus on adding locations where they are needed most, and if necessary, relax zoning laws to allow them to fit.

That’s not to say the private sector is sitting around doing nothing. In recent years, Japan has seen the emergence of what is colloquially called “itai hotels” (literally “corpse hotels”). These are facilities that refrigerate the body so it is preserved until cremation can be made available, while also allowing loved ones to visit in a respectful, home-like environment. True to the name, they even offer rates comparable to a hotel’s, ranging from 10,000 to 200,000 per day depending on size and quality.

▼ News report showing the inside of an itai hotel

The real difficulty in these projects is that, despite how serious the problem is now, it’s destined to be a temporary one because of Japan’s shrinking population, making it harder to make a case for large-scale infrastructure investment. At least if governments take the initiative in building new crematoriums, they can be shut down more easily when no longer needed, and itai hotels are more or less standard commercial facilities that can be easily repurposed.

It’s an awkward situation that Japan is still trying to feel its way around, but it’s something many other countries are going to have to face in the coming years. Hopefully, others can learn from what goes right and what goes wrong here.

title: Pachinko parlor operator arrested for not obscuring the act of gambling well enough
description: If you’re going to do wrong, do wrong right. For many years, pachinko parlors have stood tall and proud in just about every community across the country as bastions of the human desire to make quick money without having to work for it. Every day, thousands and thousands of people flock to the large and […]
content:
If you’re going to do wrong, do wrong right.

For many years, pachinko parlors have stood tall and proud in just about every community across the country as bastions of the human desire to make quick money without having to work for it. Every day, thousands and thousands of people flock to the large and comfortably equipped complexes, seemingly never realizing that the main reason these places are so large and comfortably equipped is that they’re the ones ending up with the money.

It should be noted that pachinko is technically not gambling, however. Japan has frowned on the vice of gambling for most of its history, with the exception of government-run operations of horse racing, boat racing, bicycle racing, and the lottery, as well as a recently enacted law allowing strictly managed casinos in integrated resorts.

▼ You get four forms of gambling and that’s it! OK, fine! Five, but that’s really it!

Even when pachinko players win, they get no money awarded by the parlor. Depending on the performance of the player, they are awarded metal balls by the machine. They’re kind of like the tickets you’d get from a skee-ball machine, and in the same way, you can trade in the balls at a counter in the parlor for wonderful “special prizes” (tokushu keihin). These prizes can be ordinary arbitrary items like pens or lighter flint, but many places nowadays award cards with tiny pieces of gold in them to help prevent counterfeiting.

▼ It takes a lot of balls to play this game.

As luck would have it, right beside, or at least not too far from the pachinko parlor, there is always a store owned by people who seem to really love these special prizes. If you go here, you can sell them for ridiculously more than they’re actually worth and walk away with a nice chunk of change from a legitimate sale of your newfound special prizes. It’s a bit of a silly business model if you ask me, which must be why these places are often very modest-looking and have little to no signage.

▼ On your right is a pachinko parlor and on the left is a shop that buys prizes for a pachinko parlor. It may look like the same business, but that store is technically in a different building and owned by a different company, and what’s with all the questions anyway? What, are you a cop or something?

Of course, since they offer such amazing prices for these prizes, they often end up with too many. But a lucky coincidence strikes again in the form of a wholesaler who is willing to buy those items from the shop, practically at cost, and sell them back to the pachinko parlors, once again, practically at cost. Since these are all legit sales, the government gets its piece of the action in the form of taxes, and everyone’s happy… except those players without wonderful special prizes, of whom there are many.

This circle of life is called the “santen hoshiki” or “three-store system,” and it’s what separates dirty, yucky gambling from shiny, happy free-market capitalism. But should a pachinko parlor take it upon themselves to not follow the three-store system, trouble awaits, as it did recently in Miyagi Prefecture.

On October 30th, it was reported that charges were filed against the manager and operating company of a pachinko parlor in the city of Ishinomaki. According to the charges, on 20 January, the parlor purchased four special prizes from a customer for a total of 3,500 yen (US$22), thus bypassing the three-store system and awarding cash prizes for games of chance. This parlor had since closed down, but the 71-year-old manager confessed to the act. This is the first such case to occur in Miyazaki since 2007.

Readers of the news expressed understandable confusion in comments with regard to what the heck is actually going on with pachinko in Japan in the first place.

“Seriously, why is the three-store system only permitted for pachinko parlors? Has that ever actually been explained?”
“Why go through with all this superficial nonsense? Just ban pachinko for crying out loud.”
“This is kind of absurd, isn’t it?”
“In Asakusa [in Tokyo] there’s an exchange booth for a pachinko parlor right next to a police box.”
“There’s probably some other crime involved they want to look into.”
“Funny how pachinko parlor staff never seem to notice the mysterious little shacks sitting right on their own premises.”
“The three-shop system is inherently illegal, isn’t it?”
“I’ll just go and set up my own three-shop system then.”

While it sounds like a great idea to set up your own casino and only give away prizes that can be cycled through the three-store system, that will likely land you in prison. As mentioned in the comments, this system is only applicable to pachinko and slot machines. All other games are regulated differently.

Casino games are the most highly regulated, and if the house gives out so much as a mustache comb, they’ll get shut down faster than you can say, “A mustache comb? What the f…”

Arcades, or “game centers” as they’re called in Japan, also have regulations on awarding prizes of any kind. One exception are UFO catchers, and this is mainly because in these games, the entire point is to grab the item. However, they are strictly regulated as well, and the prizes they offer cannot exceed a wholesale price of 1,000 yen per item.

▼ That’s a good fact to know when considering a lucky bag claw game.

Another interesting example of pseudo-gambling in Japan are those high-end gacha machines where you pay 1,000 yen for a chance to get a Gucci bag or PS5. The reason these aren’t gambling is because they aren’t even classified as games. They’re technically vending machines from which straight purchases are made, and they will be treated as such as long as the customer never “loses” in the sense of getting an empty capsule or booby prize.

Long-time readers of our site might remember our writer Masanuki Sunakoma getting an endless array of junk from those machines, like gearbox keychains and talon necklaces.

However, the regulation states that the item in the capsule must have a “hypothetical” retail price of what the person paid. That “hypothetical” creates a considerable grey area since a shop could hypothetically sell a bag of chips for 10,000 yen.

▼ You could argue that a shop might conceivably sell the above necklace for 1,000 yen, which is what the machine charged, but selling this plastic dinosaur for that much is really pushing it.

This brings us back to the question of why pachinko parlors get such special treatment. The game in its current quasi-gambling form was largely used as a way for Zainichi Koreans living in Japan to earn a living right after World War II, being otherwise unable to get a job at companies. The yakuza also got involved at the time, either “supporting” or “exploiting” these businesses depending how you want to look at it.

Japan was in a massive state of upheaval at the time, so there was little oversight on these parlors. As things normalized, pachinko had grown into a major pastime, and as the police became more organized, they turned their attention to it. Rather than completely shutting them down, the police opted to drive out the yakuza and allow the remaining owners to continue running their parlors. The three-store system was one method to do this, and the police installed themselves as regulators for the entire industry, again “supporting” or “exploiting” these businesses depending how you want to look at it.

By the late ’80s and ’90s, pachinko had grown into a gigantic industry that was heavily tied into the national economy and employed hundreds of thousands of workers, essentially making it too big to fail. At this point, everyone seemed to just agree that it had gone beyond the point of no return and that the thin veil of the three-store system would have to do.

However, there are serious questions as to how much longer pachinko parlors will continue as they are. With the legalization of casinos in integrated resorts, those with the gambling bug may be more attracted to the glitz and glamor of such facilities, drawing even more revenue away. Parlors are already closing at an increasing pace and may eventually die a natural death before too long, but at least all those machines can go to good use at retirement homes.

title: Continuing cyberattacks hit Japanese arcade hard [Photos]
description: Preserving arcade culture is hard enough without hacker jerks making it even tougher. A photo of an empty interior and unused game machines accompanied by the message “This is the harsh reality for arcades right now” might be the kind of thing that would make gamers sad, but not necessarily surprised. Though the video game […]
content:
Preserving arcade culture is hard enough without hacker jerks making it even tougher.

A photo of an empty interior and unused game machines accompanied by the message “This is the harsh reality for arcades right now” might be the kind of thing that would make gamers sad, but not necessarily surprised. Though the video game business as a whole is bigger than ever, the ways that people play them has changed significantly since the arcade glory days of the ‘80s and ‘90s, and the industry trend in Japan has become one of arcades steadily reducing the amount of floorspace they devote to video games while installing more and more UFO catcher/crane/claw prize machines.

But a recent tweet from the Machida branch of arcade chain Taito Station in Tokyo doesn’t show just row after row of unoccupied games, but ones with dark screens too.

ゲームセンターの過酷な現状…
お客様の皆様には大変御迷惑お掛けしています。 pic.twitter.com/gF1YjwSEZ9

— タイステ町田 (@Taito_Machida) November 5, 2026

The reason for all that dark emptiness isn’t because the arcade’s entire customer base decided they’d rather be somewhere else playing Fortnite on their phones. No, it’s because, as with so many other things these days, of the huge increase in hacks, cyberattacks, and other online maliciousness and jackassery over the past few weeks.

One of the ways the surviving arcade video game franchises have survived is by embracing online/network play, especially if it’s coupled to some sort of deluxe control or display hardware that would be impractically large or expensive for many people’s homes, such as a full steering wheel and pedals, expansive dance step sensors, card readers, or gigantic touchscreen arrays. Combine that feeling of immersion with the ability to race, fight, or otherwise compete with other players, either in real-time or through leaderboards, and you can cultivate a customer community by connecting modestly sized, geographically separated pockets of fans.

Unfortunately, that means that if a game network’s security is compromised and it has to be shut down, either in response to a hack or as a preventive measure, the game has to be shut down too. Network play is so integrated into many Japanese arcade games that the first thing they do upon booting up is try to connect to their network, and some can’t progress to a playable state until they can successfully do so, resulting in situations like the one shown in the Taito Station Machida tweet, in which the arcade says “We deeply apologize for the great inconvenience to our customers.”

一角は営業中かも危ぶまれるような写真ですがちゃんと稼働しているゲームも勿論有りますので是非ともご利用下さいね！#タイステ #町田 pic.twitter.com/bcDo1HmieB

— タイステ町田 (@Taito_Machida) November 5, 2026

Thankfully, not every game in the arcade has had to go offline, and classic titles that don’t require a network connection are unaffected, so, as shown in the above follow-up tweet, Taito Station Matsuda still has games that can be played, and they invite gamers to come in for them. Other arcades are likely dealing with similar problems, so if you’re a gamer with a few spare 100-yen coins in your wallet, they’d probably appreciate a visit, even if your regular favorites aren’t currently playable.

title: Starbucks Japan reveals this year’s lucky bag, but you’ll have to act fast to get one
description: Fukubukuro season starts very early for Starbucks fans in Japan. In Japan, shops, restaurants, and other companies celebrate the new year by releasing fukubukuro, a.k.a. lucky bags, surprise assortments of their wares and coupons, usually with a combined value much greater than their asking price. content:
Fukubukuro season starts very early for Starbucks fans in Japan.

In Japan, shops, restaurants, and other companies celebrate the new year by releasing fukubukuro, a.k.a. lucky bags, surprise assortments of their wares and coupons, usually with a combined value much greater than their asking price. Back in the day, the only way to get a lucky bag was to show up at the shop on the first few days of the year, but especially popular bags now go on sale ahead of time, and with Starbucks Japan’s lucky bag being one of the most popular of all, it’s going on sale while we’re still in November.

One of the reasons Starbucks Japan’s lucky bag is so coveted is because of the bag itself. While most other brands’ fukubukuro are disposable paper pouches, Starbucks Japan gives you a classy tote bag. The design, featuring an emblem of the Starbucks mermaid, is elegantly understated in order to coordinate with a wide variety of outfits, and sized such that it can work for both fashionable in-city meetups or more extensive outings for which you need to carry more gear.

But you can’t be a lucky bag without also having cool stuff inside. The highlight of the contents is a fukubukuro-exclusive Starbucks Japan stainless steel drink bottle, the design of which is still being kept under wraps. You’ll also receive three pieces of randomly selected Starbucks lucky bag-exclusive merch, which could be one of 1,000 special mug and Bearista plushie combos.

▼ The surprise is super lucky and super cute.

To fill up the drink bottle, the bag additionally contains two bags of Starbucks coffee, one of high-grade roast and one of light-note blend, as well as a Coffee Bean Ticket redeemable for a bag of coffee of up to 2,000 yen (US$13) at any Starbucks Japan branch. Finally, for when you’re not in the mood to do your own brewing, the bundle also contains seven drink tickets, once again redeemable at any Starbucks in Japan.

The 2027 Starbucks lucky bag is priced at 9,500 yen, but because the demand is so high for them every year, it’s offered by a pre-sale lottery system only. To enter, you’ll need to be a My Starbucks member and complete the online entry form between November 4 and November 15. Randomly selected winners will then be notified by email (Starbucks says notifications are slated to be sent out by November 25), after which payment can be arranged and you can select a delivery date between January 1 and 7 of 2027 (domestic shipping is included in the price of the fukubukuro).

The entry form can be found here. And if it’s still too early for you to be thinking about New Year’s, but not too early for you to be thinking about Christmas, Starbucks Japan has something for you too.

title: Princess Mononoke was going to look totally different, new Studio Ghibli artbook shows
description: Art collection includes never-before-shown illustrations from Hayao Miyazaki’s vision for a feudal-Japan version of Beauty and the Beast. The very first time I saw a preview for Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke, I was shocked by how dark the tone was. I was not at all prepared for a grim tale of humans and giant forest […]
content:
Art collection includes never-before-shown illustrations from Hayao Miyazaki’s vision for a feudal-Japan version of Beauty and the Beast.

The very first time I saw a preview for Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke, I was shocked by how dark the tone was. I was not at all prepared for a grim tale of humans and giant forest creatures fighting to the death in a territorial struggle with no clear “good guys” or “bad guys.” I’d been expecting this story of a mononoke/monster princess to be a sort of feudal Japan-version of Beauty and the Beast, complete with a cuddly-looking cat samurai’s caring, protective side being awoken by a young girl whose safety he has to ensure.

However, my shock wasn’t because the Princess Mononoke trailer was the first piece of Japanese animation I’d ever seen, some sort of “THIS IS ANIME!” moment that shattered my sheltered American mind with the revelation that animation didn’t have to be limited to Disney fairy tales (I’d already had that experience — thank you, Bubblegum Crisis). No, the reason I had been expecting Princess Mononoke to a pseudo-Beauty and the Beast with cute Ghibli critters is because that’s what the original story concept and artwork were, as shown way back during the anime’s pre-production phase and reprinted in at least one North American anime magazine at the time.

I’ve been telling fellow anime fans this for years, usually getting a puzzled expression and awkward silence in response, but now finally I can point to the newest entry in the Hayao Miyazaki Image Board Series, in which the early-concept artwork for Princess Mononoke has been collected.

▼ Two of these illustrations will immediately look familiar to people who’ve watched Princess Mononoke, and one of them almost certainly will not.

This is the seventh volume in publisher Iwanami Shoten’s Hayao Miyazaki Image Board Series, which compiles all of the concept illustrations and brainstorming drawings produced by anime director Studio Ghibli co-founder Hayao Miyazaki. A total of 258 pieces of artwork are contained within the 184-page book, including 90 which have never been publicly shown before, making it a sort of record of two different Princess Mononoke, the version we were originally going to get, and the one we eventually did.

Miyazaki was developing the original Beauty and the Beast-esque story after directing 1992’s Porco Rosso, and in 1993 he added text to some of his concept illustrations for a long out-of-print book, also titled Princess Mononoke, which was published by Tokuma Shoten, Studio Ghibli’s parent company. As time went by, though, Miyazaki came to feel that the story he was crafting was too old-fashioned and stale, and while working on the animated music video for Japanese pop song “On Your Mark” in 1995, he became convinced that “it is wrong to be limited by the past,” and the changes in creative course from then on were what resulted in the Princess Mononoke anime that opened in Japanese theaters in 1997.

Hayao Miyazaki Image Board Series Volume 7-Princess Mononoke, which comes with a personal endorsement by One Piece creator Eiichiro Oda (hence his signature on the book’s obi paper wrapping), goes on sale December 3, priced at 6,000 yen (US$38), and can be purchased through Iwanami Shoten ‘s website here.

title: Liquid croissant coffee is coming to Japanese stores this month
description: Suntory’s newest Craft Boss release promises the taste of freshly dunked buttery pastry in a single bottle. One of the things I’ve enjoyed since coming to Japan has been stopping at vending machines I walk past to check out what new and unusual drinks they have on offer and scouring different supermarket and convenience store […]
content:
Suntory’s newest Craft Boss release promises the taste of freshly dunked buttery pastry in a single bottle.

One of the things I’ve enjoyed since coming to Japan has been stopping at vending machines I walk past to check out what new and unusual drinks they have on offer and scouring different supermarket and convenience store shelves for limited-edition flavors that could potentially blow my mind with their outlandishness—I’m looking at you, caramel popcorn soda. Now, the latest limited-time release coming from beverage maker Suntory seems to suggest they’ve been attempting to liquidize a bakery item.

In collaboration with the popular bakery chain Bread, Espresso & and hitting shelves on November 10 for a limited time, Craft Boss Croissant Latte is an attempt to capture the exact flavor you get after dunking a croissant into a warm caffe latte.

As far as I’m aware, the French can be quite vocal about proper etiquette when it comes to their bread and coffee on the best of days, but turning the breakfast habit into a drinkable liquid in a plastic bottle might have them sharpening their baguettes for the sheer audacity.

According to the breakdown of the recipe, the drink blends light-roasted coffee beans with espresso to create a sophisticated bitterness, plus sugar, a touch of salt, and the custom croissant flavor, with a result that aims to form a buttery aroma and a multi-layered balance of sweet, bitter, and salty notes in every sip.

As with all Suntory Boss coffee varieties, we can expect to see the Croissant Latte in Japanese convenience stores and supermarkets, and it’s scheduled to go on sale November 10. Starting that same day, select 19 Bread, Espresso & stores nationwide will also be selling a special 900-yen (US$5.70) Croissant Latte menu item featuring a honey-butter caramelized croissant designed specifically for dipping into foamy latte cream.

The first 100 people at each store who order from the collaboration menu will also receive a bottle of Craft Boss Croissant Latte (limited to one per person).

title: First-ever cafe on Tokyo Imperial Palace Garden grounds is now open
description: Green oasis in the center of Tokyo is site of city’s newest cafe serving exclusive coffee blend. With people in Japan long having been fans of cafe culture, Tokyo has plenty of spots in the city in which to sit and sip a cup of coffee. However, there’s never been a cafe on the grounds […]
content:
Green oasis in the center of Tokyo is site of city’s newest cafe serving exclusive coffee blend.

With people in Japan long having been fans of cafe culture, Tokyo has plenty of spots in the city in which to sit and sip a cup of coffee. However, there’s never been a cafe on the grounds of the Imperial Palace, until now.

November 3 was the grand opening for the Imperial Palace East Garden branch of Sarutahiko Coffee. As the name implies, the cafe is inside the eastern garden area of the palace grounds, not far from Tokyo Station and open to the public, free of charge.

Sarutahiko Coffee started off as a specialty coffee shop in Tokyo’s Ebisu neighborhood, and it now operates a small chain of cafes in the capital. This new branch is special, though, and so it serves an exclusive Imperial Palace East Garden Blend, inspired by the changing seasons, beautiful plant life, and crisp air of the gardens, which for a green oasis in the city center. The dark-roast promises dark chocolate notes and the scent of violets, with the subtle flavor of grapes becoming more noticeable as the coffee cools. The light-roast, meanwhile, has impressions of caramel, orange, and cherry, and picks up a sense of tropical fruit once it cools off.

▼ In addition to coffee to drink in-store, packs of the Imperial Palace East Garden Blend can also be purchased to take home.

▼ Imperial Palace East Garden-exclusive drink bottles

A wide selection of cakes, pastries, and other desserts are also on offer, mixing both Japanese and Western confectionery traditions.

The cafe is attached to a new rest area and located across a pedestrian pathway from the Museum of the Imperial Collections, Sannomaru Shozokan, an art/history museum which also opened on November 3. Customers can enjoy their drinks on the cafe’s second-floor terrace, taking in views of the surrounding greenery…

…or at inside seating, which features tables made with hinoki (Japanese cedar) wood harvested from the same forest where Ise Shrine sources the timber for its periodic rebuilding ceremonies.

The cafe follows the same schedule as the garden, which means that it closes at dusk, but this also allows it to be extremely ecologically friendly. Because the Imperial Palace Gardens create a skyscraper-free buffer zone, they receive plenty of sunlight during the day, and the cafe can operate entirely by solar power, so you can feel good about being kind to Mother Nature as you treat yourself to a drink and a snack ina very unique location.

title: Godzilla becomes a Japanese randoseru backpack, as do two of his greatest rivals [Photos]
description: King of the Monsters looks to become lord of the backpacks. Durability and functionality are the two biggest priorities for Japan’s randoseru backpacks. The boxy bags need to be able to carry everything a student needs on their way to and from school for six years, after all. But in recent years, more and more […]
content:
King of the Monsters looks to become lord of the backpacks.

Durability and functionality are the two biggest priorities for Japan’s randoseru backpacks. The boxy bags need to be able to carry everything a student needs on their way to and from school for six years, after all.

But in recent years, more and more people are also looking for randoseru with fashionable or fun designs, and now come awesome randoseru inspired by none other than the King of the Monsters himself, Godzilla.

For this three-bag lineup, Toho, producer of the Japanese Godzilla films, is partnering with Dinosaurbase, a company in Fukui Prefecture that specializes in dinosaur-themed bags and accessories. Of course, the most crowd-pleasing Godzilla movies are the ones where more than one kaiju joins the battle, so in addition to a Godzilla randoseru, the collection also includes backpacks honoring King Ghidoroah and Mechagodzilla.

While the overall construction is the same, each backpack features a different texturing. Though Godzilla is essentially a giant lizard, his skin is an irregular pattern of ridges, and that’s reflected on the outer surface of his bag.

King Ghidorah, meanwhile, does have serpentine scales, recreated in his regal gold color…

…and the Mechagodzilla model takes its cures from the robot’s armor plating.

Open up the flap, and you’ll find an intimidating portrait of each kaiju on the underside. Godzilla and Mechagodzilla both appear as they did in their debut films, the original 1954 Godzilla and 1974’s Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla. Kind Ghidorah, however, is depicted not as he was in his 1964 rookie outing Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster, but in his form seen in Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, which came out in Japanese theaters in 1991.

With the flap open, each kaiju’s name appears, written in stylized Japanese script, on the outer surface of one of the zippered pockets.

The terrifying and territorial trio also manage to get along well enough to share space on a metallic side hook, with color coordination matching the main kaiju’s image hue.

Each of them goes solo, though, for their bag’s zipper pulls…

…as well as for the lenticular image crests on the front of each shoulder strap that show them unleashing their destructive powers.

The bags are identically sized, with exterior dimensions of 23.5 x 31 x 13.5 centimeters (9.3 x 12.2 x 5.3 inches), and the squared off central compartment helps keeps textbooks and notebooks neatly stacked.

Randoseru are customarily carried in Japan by elementary school students, but the bags’ designers say that these are not only for kids entering the first grade, but also for “Godzilla fans across the nation,” implying that they know that there’ll be grown-up kaiju enthusiasts who might want one of these too. They are still made with the high-grade materials and craftsmanship that Japanese consumers demand of randoseru, and the commensurate price of 93,500 yen (US$590). Pre-orders open through the Dinosaurbase website here on January 23, but the bags are slated to ship for the start of the 2028 Japanese school year (which begins in spring), so you’ve still got some time to mull over whether this is a fashion statement you’re willing to commit to.

title: Japan’s free stock image site of muscular men doing whimsical and mundane things reveals rankings
description: The site with a goal of “Adding muscles to everyday life” has released a new gallery collecting its most viral muscly moments up to the present.  Fukuoka-based Smile Academy’s Muscle Plus free stock image site has been around for a while now and it hasn’t stopped causing a stir. We can only thank the muscular […]
content:
The site with a goal of “Adding muscles to everyday life” has released a new gallery collecting its most viral muscly moments up to the present. 

Fukuoka-based Smile Academy’s Muscle Plus free stock image site has been around for a while now and it hasn’t stopped causing a stir. We can only thank the muscular geniuses who decided to gift the world with free-to-use, professional-quality shots of themselves posing in situations that make you think, “Heck, I can’t use that for anything!” before immediately downloading it anyway. Their purpose is not only making viewers’ smile muscles move but also promoting local people, cultural artifacts, events, and places in rural Fukuoka Prefecture in an effort to revitalize the area. Much of their work is seasonally appropriate as well, as seen in the epic Halloween photo story collection a few years back.

▼ Logo for the Muscle Plus free stock image site

Thanks to the positive public response, Muscle Plus has just released a new page that collects the photos and some quantitative data behind its most trending photos on Twitter. Thanks to this new system, you can simply check out which photos are getting the most hits when you’re in need of an image with impact. Below, we’ve compiled five of the top trending photos along with the date when they were uploaded to Twitter and their cumulative likes and views. All numbers are accurate as of October 21, 2026, so many have likely gained more hits since then.

1. Uploaded to Twitter on September 26, 2026
123,553 likes / 9,337,570 views

There’s nothing quite as refreshing as two buff dudes frolicking in a field of vibrantly pink cosmos in Nokonoshima Park. This would be a peak tourism campaign if we ever saw one.

2. Uploaded October 1, 2026
52,535 likes / 2,170,577 views

Two guys demonstrate how to harvest tea leaves at Yame Central Tea Plantation. It’s not a technique that we’ve ever seen before, but they seem to know what they’re doing.

94,684 likes / 3,594,236 views

This quintessential summertime shot in the sunflower field at Fukufuku no Sato farmers’ market reminds us that it’s OK to stop and sniff the flowers–sans shirts–sometimes.

109,505 likes / 6,548,394 views

Have you ever been sitting there eating some delicious yakiimo on a crisp autumn day with your weightlifting buddies when a cat suddenly decides to crash the photoshoot? No, it’s never happened to us, but we’re very thankful it happened to them.

5. Uploaded December 25, 2022

We just hate it when we’re baking in the kitchen at Patisserie Serenite and someone comes along and sneakily adds liquid protein to the freshly whipped cream we were making. Thank goodness there’s a stock image to capture that situation.

The dudes at Muscle Plus have almost gotten us excited enough to start our own library of free stock images–though in our case, there would be much less of the buff and more of the puff.

title: Thief mails 46 million-yen watch back to Tokyo store he stole it from, says “I’m sorry”
description: Latest crook to hit Tokyo’s hottest theft target feels either remorse or fear, but probably shouldn’t expect forgiveness. In a city as big as Tokyo, different neighborhoods have different atmospheres, but those reputations can change over time. For example, Nakano is best known for its Nakano Broadway shopping center, which used to be thought of […]
content:
Latest crook to hit Tokyo’s hottest theft target feels either remorse or fear, but probably shouldn’t expect forgiveness.

In a city as big as Tokyo, different neighborhoods have different atmospheres, but those reputations can change over time. For example, Nakano is best known for its Nakano Broadway shopping center, which used to be thought of almost entirely as a place for fans of eclectic pop and subculture genres, sort of like a weirder, less trendy version of Akihabara. Over the last few years, though, Nakano Broadway has become famous for having a dense concentration of luxury wristwatch stores, stocked with both new and used high-demand models.

Sadly, Nakano Broadway’s reputation is continuing to evolve, and it’s now becoming a place known for attracting not only watch fans, but watch thieves too. On the evening of October 29, a man, at the time seemingly an interested shopper, approached a salesperson inside a watch store in Nakano Broadway and asked if he could try on a piece that was in a locked showcase. The salesperson obliged, and the man slipped on a watch from Swiss brand Audemars Piguet, only to suddenly run off with it still on his wrist. And while the man hadn’t been an actual shopper, he apparently still knew a thing or two about watches, as the model he stole has a price of 46 million yen (approximately US$290,000).

▼ A CG reenactment of the crime

After fleeing the building, the man escaped out into the web of narrow streets that twist around Nakano Broadway. However, this is still a fairly developed part of Tokyo, not the sort of place where a sprinting thief can blend in with fitness joggers, but Nakano also isn’t so dense one can easily disappear into a sea of passersby either. As a result, investigators were able to spot the fleeing man in recording from multiple security cameras, as shown in the video here.

▼ The video also shows the model of watch that was stolen.

Though the thief is still at large (as of this writing), the stolen watch has been returned, and, surprisingly, it was the thief himself who returned it, via a takuhaibin/parcel delivery service. On the morning of November 1, a cardboard box which had been mailed from Aichi Prefecture was delivered to the store that was robbed, and when the staff opened it, they found a watch matching the model and serial number of the one that was stolen, plus a handwritten letter of apology that included the statement “I’m sorry.” The watch doesn’t appear to have suffered any noticeable damage during its time away from the store.

Online reactions to the unexpected turn of events have included:

“Must have realized it was only a matter of time until they caught him.”
“Okay, so he got spooked and returned the watch. He still stole it.”
“Returning it doesn’t undo the crime. Turn yourself in.”
“It’s like he thinks they’ll just treat it as a prank since he the watch back.”
“If you know you should return it, you should have known not to take it in the first place.”
“Thieves have totally marked Nakano Broadway.”
“If they’re going to let people try on watches that are that expensive, they should make them do it in a locked room.”

With law-abiding citizens in Japan still fuming over a different brazen watch robbery that recently took place at Nakano Broadway, it’s not surprising that public sentiment isn’t leaning towards letting the guy off the hook just because he returned the property that he stole. Japan is, after all, the country that says “If everything could be solved by saying ‘sorry,’ we wouldn’t need police,” and investigators are still searching for the thief.

title: This is Japan’s best cycling course, but is it fun for bicycling beginners too?
description: We head to the Seto Inland Sea for a Shimanami Kaido sampler. Japan has a lot of great places for bicycling, but the Shimanami Kaido Cycling Road is widely considered to be the best. Stretching across the Seto Inland Sea, the 70-kilometer (43.5-mile) route ties together seven different islands as it runs from the town […]
content:
We head to the Seto Inland Sea for a Shimanami Kaido sampler.

Japan has a lot of great places for bicycling, but the Shimanami Kaido Cycling Road is widely considered to be the best. Stretching across the Seto Inland Sea, the 70-kilometer (43.5-mile) route ties together seven different islands as it runs from the town of Imabari in Ehime Prefecture on Shikoku all the way to Onomichi, Hiroshima Prefecture on Japan’s main island of Honshu.

But while the idea of a 70-kilomter, possibly multi-day ride sounds fun for dedicated cyclists, is it possible for beginner-level bicyclists to enjoy the Shimanami Kaido too, even if they can’t devote a whole day to it? That was the question our Japanese-language reporter Saya Togashi found herself asking. Saya lives in a fairly rural part of Japan, and the lack of public transportation means that she spends pretty much every day getting around by car. Sure, she knows how to ride a bike, but it’s not something she does very often, and certainly not to the extent that she’s built up a fitness cyclist’s musculature and stamina.

And yet, Saya could still feel the Shimanami Kaido calling to her, and her initial research suggested that while the course is loved by serious cyclists, it’s very accommodating to novices as well. For starters, there are 10 official rental cycle depots along the route, so there’s no need to bring your own bike. Depending on the type of bike and specific location, some of the depots even allow you to drop off your bike at a different spot than where you started your ride, in case you want to go part-way across the islands on bike, then do the rest by car, bus, or boat.

Saya decided to get her bike at the Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle depot in Imabari, essentially the southernmost tip of the Shimanami Kaido. It’s possible (and, honestly, advisable) to reserve a bike ahead of time, but Saya hadn’t made any such arrangements. Nevertheless, when she showed up at around 10 a.m. on a weekday, they still had plenty of bikes available, even some electric-assist ones like the one Saya picked out, which cost 4,000 yen (US$25) for one day.

▼ Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle also provides helmets free of charge.

Instead of the full-course Shimanami Kaido, Saya’s plan was to experience the first section, sort of an appetizer-size version. Since Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle has a free parking lot, she could leave her car there while she was pedaling and take her time without worrying about racking up expensive parking fees.

After Saya selected her bike, the staff adjusted the seat height for her and pointed her towards the nearby bridge that makes up the start of the course. They also explained that you can tell when you’re following the Shimanami Kaido by the blue lines marked on the pavement, so there’s no fear of getting lost.

This first bridge, called the Kurushima Kaikyo Bridge, is less than 10 minutes from the rental cycle depot, and it’s a very big piece of infrastructure, about 50 meters (164 feet) up above the shoreline. The bike path, though, spirals around on the way up to keep the incline from getting all that steep, and especially if you’re using an electric-assist bike, it’s not so strenuous, even for a beginner like Saya.

The high guard rails were also reassuring, keeping Saya and her bike separated from car traffic on one side and safe from the drop-off down to the sea on the other. The peace of mind they provided left Saya with the necessary mental space to appreciate just how beautiful the view is from up here.

The weather was a little cloudy on this day, but that added to the atmosphere, and also meant the sun wasn’t beating down on her with full force. There are so many islands in this part of Japan that sometimes they look like they’re layered on top of one another. On the closer ones Saya could make out individual houses and other buildings, while the ones farther in the distance, wrapped in a light mist, looked like they could be part of an ink seascape painting.

Though she’d worked up a bit of a sweat, Saya was making steady progress, and had a smile on her face with no stress in her heart. She felt like she’d sprouted wings as she smoothly zoomed ahead to the far side of the bridge…

…though she stopped for a bit at a cyclist rest area, not because she was worn out, but to snap a few more photos and bask in the cool sea breeze for a bit.

Once you come down on the other side of the bridge, you’re still in Imabari City, but now on the island of Oshima, in a picturesque coastal community.

Following the blue line in the road brought Saya to Yoshiumi Ikiiki Hall, the island’s michi no eki/”roadside station,” a center for local foods and handicrafts. Bringing her bike to stop and heading into the food court, Saya spotted several other cyclists who were biking the Shimanami Kaido in whole or in part, and she decided to fuel up with a fish sandwich, a sausage one…

…and, of course, some soft serve ice cream.

This was as far as Saya was planning to ride today, but rather than rushing straight back to Imabari Itoyama Rental Cycle, she stopped by the Oshima port along the way, which offers short sightseeing cruises on the Seto Inland Sea.

In total, Saya covered around six kilometers on her round-trip ride from the rental cycle depot over to Oshima and back, and spent around an hour and a half pedaling. This is, she admits, only a very small portion of the Shimanami Kaido, but she still feels like it was enough to understand what makes the course so fun. In addition to experienced bicycling buffs doing the whole thing, she also saw people like herself who were clearly just doing a part of it. She saw people of different ages and backgrounds, and even from different countries, all enjoying this unique activity, creating a heartwarming sense of comradery, and at one point when she got off her bike to readjust the seat, a passing cyclist stopped to make sure she wasn’t in any sort of mechanical distress.

So yes, Saya is happy to report that you don’t have to go hard-core to enjoy going along part of the Shimanami Kaido. Maybe she’ll eventually cycle the whole thing, broken up into different segments on different trips, but if and when she, or you, are ready to go all the way from one end to the other, we’ve got a report on what that’s like too.
